item.title: Mufin Green Finance To Acquire 23% Stake In BimaPay For ₹66 Cr
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Listed non-banking financial company (NBFC) Mufin Green Finance’s board has approved the acquisition of a 23% stake in insurtech startup…
item.content:encoded:
Listed non-banking financial company (NBFC) Mufin Green Finance’s board has approved the acquisition of a 23% stake in insurtech startup BimaPay for a ₹65.8 Cr in an all-cash deal. 

Mufin Green Finance said that it expects to complete the transaction in the next three to four months, subject to the execution of definitive agreements and relevant regulatory approvals. It is pertinent to note that BimaPay operates under the umbrella of the broader Mufin Group. 

“…. With an RBI-registered NBFC as a shareholder, we can build products around how lending actually works rather than adapt them later,” said BimaPay cofounder and CEO Hanut Mehta. 

In a statement, Mufin said that he proposed investment will leverage synergies between the two entities and support the joint development and scaling of premium financing solutions. The transaction will look to combine the listed NBFC’s lending expertise with BimaPay’s tech solutions. 

“… An ownership stake lets us plan product, data and integration roadmaps over years instead of project cycles, which is what a lender growing at our pace needs,” added Mufin Green Finance managing director Kapil Garg said.

The deal is a related-party transaction as Bimapay is a promoter-group subsidiary of Mufin, the listed NBFC said.

Founded in 2022 by Mehta, Mohit Gupta and Kapil Garg, BimaPay facilitates financing solutions to enable individuals and businesses to pay insurance premiums in EMIs instead of upfront lump sums. It also works with lending partners and insurers to develop technology-enabled solutions.

The startup last raised $2 Mn in an undisclosed funding round led by LC Nueva Investment Partners in 2024.

On the financial front BimaPay reported revenue of ₹9.9 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), up 203% from ₹3.2 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. According to Mufin Green Finance, the startup also reported a profit before tax (PBT) of ₹1.1 Cr in FY26. 

BimaPay operates at the intersection of lending tech and insurtech. The two segments are seeing healthy growth on the back of rising smartphone adoption, expanding credit and the rise of AI-driven distribution solutions.

According to Inc42 data, the Indian insurtech market is projected to become a $307 Bn opportunity by 2030.

item.title: PW To Set Up Digital University To Offer UG & PG Courses
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Moving beyond test preparation, listed edtech major PhysicsWallah (PW) has now said that it is establishing a “greenfield digital” university. …
item.content:encoded:
Moving beyond test preparation, listed edtech major PhysicsWallah (PW) has now said that it is establishing a “greenfield digital” university. 

In an investor presentation, the edtech platform said that the digital university has already been notified by the Punjab government. The digital university plans to offer 16 undergraduate, postgraduate, diploma and certificate courses including BCA, BBA, B.Com, BA, M.Com, MCA, MBA, among others. 

The edtech major also claimed that the nearly 15,000 sq ft campus will be self-financed and will operate on an asset-light model. Admissions are slated to begin in July 2027. The listed company has opted for a digital delivery model that pairs online degrees with competitive exam preparation (such as B.Com-CA and BA-UPSC combinations).

“After Class 12, many learners take a degree elsewhere. PWDU (PW digital university) keeps them with PW, from exam prep to a degree to a career,” read the presentation. 

PW has received authorisation from the state government under the “Punjab Private Digital Open Universities Policy”. The digital university will have a 3 acre physical campus, but it will serve only as the headquarters for administrative purposes. No regular classes will be held on campus.

The announcement came on the same day as the company’s maiden Investor Day in Mumbai. At the event, the company outlined an ambitious target of ₹9,000 Cr to ₹10,000 Cr in revenue by fiscal year 2029-30 (FY30). This implies a 2.5X jump from the ₹3,900 Cr top line that the company reported in FY26

The company expects this growth surge to come on the back of its online business, which it projects will contribute around “two-thirds” of its total revenue by FY30.

At its maiden Investor Day in Mumbai, the edtech giant said that it expects its revenue to rise ‌at ⁠an compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 25% between FY27 and FY30. It is also targeting an EBITDA ​margin of over 20% by ​FY30.

“Our FY30 ambition is about profit growing faster than revenue. We will stay disciplined with capital and report our progress every year,” said PhysicsWallah chief financial officer (CFO) Amit Sachdeva.

Over the next three to five years, PW plans to focus on premiumisation to drive higher average revenue per user (ARPU), leverage AI to drive efficiencies, scale vernacular courses and tap into the pre-foundation (Class 6 to Class 8) and upskilling markets.

The bullish outlook comes as PW reported a consolidated net profit of ₹143.6 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 106% from ₹69.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, revenue from operations also rose 18.2% to ₹1,242.3 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹1,051.3 Cr in Q2 FY26.

item.title: Omnichannel Fashion Brand Style Union Bags ₹485 Cr To Expand Store Network
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Omnichannel fast fashion brand Style Union’s parent Nexon Omniverse Ltd has raised ₹485 Cr (nearly $51.8 Mn) in its Series…
item.content:encoded:
Omnichannel fast fashion brand Style Union’s parent Nexon Omniverse Ltd has raised ₹485 Cr (nearly $51.8 Mn) in its Series E funding round co-led by Venturi Partners and Elev8 Venture Partners.

In a statement, the platform said that the round comprised both primary and secondary components. Style Union plans to utilise the fresh capital to expand its offline store network across key metros in West and North India.

“This is a defining moment for Nexon Omniverse and for Style Union… With their backing, we will take Style Union beyond its southern base into West and North India and into millions of new households across the country.” said Nexon Omniverse whole-time director Rajesh Seth.

Founded in 2022 by former operations head of Future Retail Rakesh Biyani and his wife Ekta Biyani, Style Union sells apparels for men, women and kids through its own website as well as offline stores. With its core footprint in South India, the brand operates 200 physical stores across Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, among other cities. 

The platform claims to have closed FY26 with over ₹1,150 Cr in revenue. It competes with the likes of Tata-owned Zudio, V-Mart and Vishal Mega Mart.

The funding comes as a growing number of Indian D2C fashion and lifestyle brands are expanding beyond online channels and building omnichannel businesses. Startups are increasingly using physical stores to improve brand discovery and customer experience while continuing to leverage ecommerce for scale.

On the back of this, the space continues to attract healthy investor interest. In September this year, D2C fashion and accessories brand Theater bagged ₹75 Cr in its Series A round led by investment firm Niveshaay. Earlier this year in March, omnichannel streetwear brand Bonkers Corner also raised $15 Mn to fuel its offline expansion plans.

Prior to this in January, D2C lifestyle brand Salty also raised ₹30 Cr to expand its product portfolio and set up a flagship store.

At the heart of all this is the homegrown fashion ecommerce space, which is projected to become a $112 Bn opportunity by 2030.

item.title: Boba Bhai Bags $18 Mn To Build A Multi-Brand QSR Chain
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Quick service restaurant (QSR) chain Boba Bhai has raised $18 Mn (about ₹168 Cr) in its Series B funding round…
item.content:encoded:
Quick service restaurant (QSR) chain Boba Bhai has raised $18 Mn (about ₹168 Cr) in its Series B funding round led by US-based Left Lane Capital. The round also saw participation from BIG Capital as well as existing backers including Titan Capital. 

Speaking with Inc42, founder Dhruv Kohli said that the round comprised both a primary deal and a small secondary component.

The fresh capital will primarily be deployed towards store expansion, strengthening its senior leadership team and building new consumer food brands under Boba Bhai Ventures.

“Expansion is the sole priority. As we have more capital now, we will double down on existing markets while also entering new markets,” Kohli said.

The latest fundraise comes months after Boba Bhai raised ₹40 Cr in its Series A round in March this year, which was co-led by 8i Ventures, Titan Capital Winners Fund and Global Growth Capital.

Founded in 2023 by Kohli, Boba Bhai is a QSR brand built around Korean delicacies like bubble tea, fusion burgers, ice cream, and fries. It claims to have expanded to 120 locations across India and serves around 3.5 Lakh orders every month. The brand also operates in tier II markets such as Lucknow, Jaipur and Kanpur.

With the latest capital infusion, Boba Bhai aims to more than double its store network to 250-300 outlets over the next 12 months. Kohli identified Kolkata, Ahmedabad and Chandigarh as key markets that Boba Bhai plans to enter over the next three to six months. It will also look at expanding into more tier II and tier III markets, including Nashik.

Boba Bhai currently has its largest store presence in Bengaluru, while Mumbai and Karnal are among its strongest markets in terms of consumer traction, Kohli said.

The startup is also expanding its product portfolio. On the QSR side, the brand claims to have introduced new ramen variants, including Shoyu, peanut and chilli flavours, alongside different protein options such as chicken, vegetarian and mushroom. Ramen currently contributes around 5-5.5% of Boba Bhai’s overall sales. 

On the FMCG side, Boba Bhai has expanded beyond beverages with a snacks range, including Korean chips. The products are being distributed through quick commerce platforms, with the startup recently launching its chips on Blinkit across five cities. 

Boba Bhai is currently clocking nearly 1,500 orders per day via quick commerce channel, said Kohli, adding that the startup now plans to expand its quick commerce presence further.

Building A Multi-Brand F&B Chain

Beyond its flagship Korean-inspired F&B brand, Boba Bhai is also looking to build a broader QSR platform through Boba Bhai Ventures.

The startup has already launched its second brand, Oreco Mexican Kitchen, with two outlets in Bengaluru. The brand is currently in the trial and testing phase, with plans to expand based on consumer response.

Unlike Boba Bhai, which focuses on Korean street food and bubble tea, Oreco will operate as a separate Mexican food brand with its own outlets, team and identity, while remaining under the same parent entity.

Kohli said the startup identified Mexican food as an opportunity to cater to different consumption occasions. While Boba Bhai’s Korean offerings see demand during snack time, evenings, dinner and late-night occasions, the startup saw an opportunity to build a brand catering to lunch consumption.

The founder added that Boba Bhai Ventures could eventually house one or two more large QSR brands, with the potential to scale each to 500-600 outlets.

The startup, however, does not plan to enter categories such as biryani, pizza or traditional Indian food. Instead, it intends to focus on global cuisines and brands targeted at younger Indian consumers.

Kohli also said Boba Bhai would prioritise formats that are not dependent on specialised chefs, allowing it to standardise food preparation and maintain consistency across a large store network.

“We don’t want to build a hotel or restaurant. We want to build a QSR where a 15-year-old can come in and still make the food taste the same,” he said.

Boba Bhai’s FY26 Snapshot

On the financial front, Boba Bhai reported a 145% jump in net revenue to around ₹70 Cr in FY26 from ₹28 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Its net loss, however, widened 32% to ₹12.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹9.5 Cr in FY25.

The startup’s growth was driven by an equal contribution from food and beverages, with both categories accounting for around 50% of revenue in FY26. It also recorded same-store sales growth of 30-40% during the fiscal.

Kohli said Boba Bhai has already crossed its entire FY26 revenue in the first half of FY27. The startup is currently clocking around ₹12.5 Cr in monthly revenue and has been growing 10-15% month-on-month, depending on seasonality.

In terms of channel mix, offline sales account for around 35% of revenue, while online channels contribute nearly 60%, according to the founder.

Kohli attributed the startup’s growth to execution, changing consumer eating-out habits and the timing of its entry into the market.

He believes the Korean food and bubble tea market in India remains largely fragmented, with no specialised player having scaled beyond 30-40 stores. While several restaurants offer bubble tea and Korean food as part of their wider menus, he believes there is room for organised, category-focused brands to build a larger presence.

Boba Bhai aims to eventually build a network of 1,000 stores in India. Our existing store network, supply-chain relationships and understanding of viable retail locations could help us expand faster, Kohli said.

Responding to a question about rising commodity prices, Kohli claimed that Boba Bhai remains largely self-sufficient in its domestic supply chain and does not expect geopolitical tensions to materially affect its operations.

item.title: Breach At External Vendor Exposes CoinDCX User Data
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: CoinDCX has informed its customers that unauthorised access at the crypto exchange’s messaging vendor Plotline exposed data of a “small…
item.content:encoded:
CoinDCX has informed its customers that unauthorised access at the crypto exchange’s messaging vendor Plotline exposed data of a “small number” of users last month.

For context, Plotline is a third-party vendor that CoinDCX uses to send in-app messages and notifications. 

In an email sent to the users, the platform said that breach occurred in two separate instances. The first incident occurred between October 24 and 26, and then again between October 30 and 31.

The crypto exchange, citing information available from Plotline, said that the data breach involved was limited to a “small number” of customers. As per the email, the unauthorised party accessed the names, email IDs and the names of banks added to users’ CoinDCX accounts. 

It did not disclose the number of affected users or specify whether any data was downloaded, copied or shared further. The exchange, however, informed the users that Plotline had no access to its internal databases, trade execution engines or user wallets. 

CoinDCX also reiterated that customer funds and wallets were “entirely secure and untouched”.

In a statement sent to Inc42, a CoinDCX spokesperson said, “Plotline, our third-party messaging vendor, experienced a security incident that exposed limited user contact details. CoinDCX’s systems and customer funds were not impacted at all. We have informed affected users and are strengthening our vendor risk controls”.

In its email to the users, CoinDCX also said it worked closely with Plotline to confirm that the incident had been fully contained. It has also initiated a review of Plotline’s security posture, data-minimisation practices and its internal vendor-risk processes.

The email did not identify the nature of the unauthorised access and the attacker. The incident comes as third-party service providers come under scrutiny amid a surge in AI-assisted cyberattacks. By writing exploit code on the fly and allowing threat actors to probe thousands of targets simultaneously, AI is drastically compressing the time between discovering a flaw and weaponising it.

This comes weeks after cryptocurrency exchange Binance also reported a major security breach, which impacted an estimated $6.3 Bn in assets. Earlier this month, researchers also flagged a malware at digital experience platform (DXP) Optimizely, which exposed visitors to potential theft of cryptocurrency, payment card details and browser data.

Earlier this month, India’s cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In also issued a critical warning to entities in the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector over an escalating campaign of AI-driven cyberattacks targeting payment and disbursement APIs.

item.title: AI Is Supercharging Cyberattacks, But Are Indian Enterprises Ready?
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: It has been a week of outages. From big tech giants like Microsoft and Apple to JPMorgan Chase and the…
item.content:encoded:
It has been a week of outages. From big tech giants like Microsoft and Apple to JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), high-profile disruptions at key digital installations exposed how fragile the global digital infrastructure could be. 

While these incidents have not yet been established as AI-assisted cyberattacks, Nikesh Arora, CEO of Palo Alto Networks, one of the world’s largest cybersecurity companies, said that the events of week were far from a coincidence.

“So what the (cybersecurity) industry tried to warn enterprises about six months ago is here. The events of this week so far are not a coincidence. AI is making it easy for hackers to attack multiple customers,” said Arora in post on X.

Besides AI-assisted cyberattacks, he also blamed some of the outages on the a “deluge of patches” from vendors rushing to fix AI-discovered vulnerabilities. Noting that this “deluge” of patches was overwhelming IT teams, he urged the enterprises to test infrastructure across multiple AI models and revamp security operations centres.

His comments brought the spotlight back on the growing threat of AI-led cyberattacks. By automating reconnaissance, writing exploit code on the fly and allowing threat actors to probe thousands of targets simultaneously, AI is drastically compressing the time between discovering a flaw and weaponising it – leaving human defenders struggling to keep pace.

With new vulnerabilities surfacing every single day, how is AI making it harder for enterprises to keep pace with cyberattackers?

Cyberattacks In The AI Era

Cybersecurity expert Ritesh Bhatia, founder of cybersecurity platform V4WEB, believes that AI is not necessarily making cyberattacks more sophisticated. Instead, he says that the technology is accelerating techniques that attackers have been using for years.

According to him, the change is primarily visible in three areas: speed, scale and realism.

Tasks that earlier took days or months can now be completed in seconds, minutes or hours. Generative AI (GenAI) has also made phishing emails more convincing by eliminating grammatical errors that could previously alert recipients. Voice cloning and deepfakes further allow attackers to impersonate senior executives and issue fraudulent instructions.

Bhatia also flagged the problem of what he described as “shadow infrastructure” or “shadow assets” at large enterprises – systems that remain untracked, forgotten or outside regular IT monitoring. AI-assisted scanning can help attackers identify vulnerabilities in these overlooked systems, he adds.

Third-party vendors are another concern. Even large enterprises with strong cybersecurity teams often depend on smaller service providers that may not have comparable security capabilities. These vendors can become easier targets, particularly as AI lowers the barrier to learning hacking techniques.

“What previously required multiple individuals with specialised skills can now increasingly be handled by a single attacker. The bigger concern is the scale at which these operations can be replicated across organisations,” said Manohar Reddy Pagilla, threat researcher at CloudSEK.

He also added that the recent outages have highlighted the concentration risk across the global technology ecosystem. Pagilla further adds that from an attacker’s perspective, compromising a technology provider serving hundreds of organisations can be more rewarding than targeting each business individually.

Yet, the threat is no longer confined to external third-party vendors. As enterprises race to embed AI into their own workflows, they are inadvertently also expanding their exposure to cyberattacks from within.

The Widening Enterprise Attack Surface

Within enterprises, AI is opening up new fronts of vulnerability: accelerating how fast bug-laden software is shipped while simultaneously supercharging how quickly its code can be broken.

Developers can now generate and deploy vast volumes of code with minimal human scrutiny. This has increased the odds of critical flaws (in authentication, payment logic, and API integrations) slipping into production before being adequately reviewed.

Attackers, meanwhile, are using the same technology to probe multiple weaknesses at once, reverse-engineer applications, and map out attack paths in a fraction of the time it once took.

“The same capabilities that make our security testing faster can also make attackers substantially more effective,” said founder and CTO of Security Brigade Yash Kadakia.

Compounding the issue of unvetted code is the rapid spread of AI across day-to-day business operations, a trend Akshit Kaushik, cofounder and CBO of Mitigata, flags as a major new blind spot.

Enterprises are increasingly entrusting AI systems to handle customer queries, process refunds, generate code, and access internal databases. At the same time, employees are independently adopting unapproved “shadow AI” tools, often completely out of sight of security teams.

Every new integration creates a fresh entry point. Kaushik warns that attackers can hide malicious instructions inside seemingly routine emails and documents, manipulating enterprise AI assistants into leaking sensitive data or executing unauthorised actions.

To close these expanding gaps, he believes businesses must establish strict visibility and governance – tracking every AI tool deployed internally, auditing the data these systems can access, and ensuring their AI systems operate strictly within defined boundaries.

What Should Indian Enterprises Do?

For India, where banking, real-time payments, telecommunications, power, and public services are built on deeply interconnected digital infrastructure, the margin for error is shrinking fast. 

Security experts suggest that Indian enterprises must move beyond traditional perimeter defense and focus on three core pillars:

Sovereign Resilience and System Modernisation: Kaushal Bheda, director at Pelorus Technologies, warns that India’s reliance on foreign software and cloud platforms for critical infrastructure introduces a distinct layer of geopolitical and supply-chain risk. 

To insulate sensitive infrastructure, he believes that Indian enterprises should aggressively upgrade legacy systems, continuously monitor networks, and invest in indigenous security products designed and controlled within the country.

Proactive Cyber Hygiene and Threat Hunting: CloudSEK’s Pagilla advises organisations to immediately lock down their most common entry points: exposed credentials, unpatched internet-facing assets, excessive access permissions, and third-party vendor vulnerabilities. 

Rather than relying solely on internal alerts, he recommends augmenting existing security operations centres (SOCs) with external threat intelligence to detect and neutralise threats before they breach internal networks.

Board-Level Incident Readiness: V4WEB’s Bhatia argues that Indian companies must shift their mindset from pure prevention to inevitable recovery. “Death, taxes and cyberhacks are bound to happen,” he noted. 

According to Bhatia, Indian enterprises should regularly test data backups, rehearse restoration protocols and preparing clear crisis-communication playbooks for customers, partners, regulators and stock exchanges.

“Today, the most important thing that companies should prioritise is incident response. When an incident happens, don’t think that it won’t happen. Are you ready to respond to it? Are you resilient enough? Have you tested your backups? Are you able to restore them?” added Bhatia.

For Indian enterprises, therefore, the question is no longer simply whether AI can make cyberattacks more effective. It is whether their security teams, infrastructure, and leadership can respond at the exact same speed.

item.title: PB Fintech Cofounder Alok Bansal To Step Down From Executive Role
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Listed insurtech giant PB Fintech’s cofounder Alok Bansal is stepping down as the executive vice-chairman and whole-time director of the…
item.content:encoded:
Listed insurtech giant PB Fintech’s cofounder Alok Bansal is stepping down as the executive vice-chairman and whole-time director of the company. 

In a statement, the company said that Bansal’s tenure will expire on March 31, 2027. PB Fintech also said that he will be appointed as a non-executive director on the company’s board starting April 1, 2027, subject to shareholder approval.

In his resignation letter, Bansal cited his “personal desire” to step down from executive responsibilities as the reason for his departure. 

“PB Fintech and Policybazaar would not have been possible without Alok. He first shared his wish to step back five years ago, and I persuaded him to stay because I needed his support. I still do, and I am glad he will remain on our Board, while I understand his wish to step away from the day-to-day…,” said PB Fintech cofounder and CEO Yashish Dahiya.

Reminiscing on his 18 year-long tenure at the company, Bansal said, “… Founders are lucky to get most of the credit and sometimes, a few brickbats as well, but the reality is that it takes the collective energies of the team to build something meaningful. PB Fintech has achieved far greater scale than I ever imagined, thanks entirely to the dedication of our team, the trust of our customers, and the support of our investors and partners”.

An alumnus of IIM Calcutta, Bansal previously served at companies like Voltas, General Electric and Mahindra & Mahindra. He eventually cofounded Policybazaar (later PB Fintech) with Dahiya in 2008. 

Over his nearly two decades stint at the company, he oversaw the company’s rise into a multi-vertical insurtech company that closed Q2 FY27 with a net profit of ₹192.4 Cr and an operating revenue of ₹2,177.7 Cr. In a statement, the startup said that he was central to the company’s strategy, fundraising and investor relations, especially during its public listing in 2021.

The development comes amid a broader wave of cofounders quitting their startups and venture capital (VC) firms. Earlier this month, Unacademy Gaurav Munjal said that he was stepping down as the CEO of the edtech platform. Prior to this, Fireside Ventures’ cofounder and partner Vinay Singh also announced his departure from the investment firm after a nearly decade-long stint.

In June this year, cofounders Hari Menon and Vipul Parekh stepped down from their executive roles at the Tata Digital-owned BigBasket. In the same month, fintech platform Setu’s cofounder Nikhil Kumar resigned from the day-to-day operations of the Pine Labs-owned platform.

In April, used car marketplace Cars24’s cofounder and chief marketing officer (CMO) Gajendra Jangid also resigned from his executive role at the startup.

item.title: Botsync Raises $11 Mn To Connect Robots And Machines On Factory Floors
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Singapore-based robotics startup Botsync has raised $11 Mn (about ₹103 Cr) in a funding round led by IvyCap Ventures to…
item.content:encoded:
Singapore-based robotics startup Botsync has raised $11 Mn (about ₹103 Cr) in a funding round led by IvyCap Ventures to upgrade its factory automation software and mobile robots. It also plans to expand its engineering and project delivery teams in India to support deployments globally.

Capital 2B, AppWorks, Iterative, AngelCentral, Genesis Alternate Investments, and angel investor Nalin Advani also participated in the funding round, which followed the startup’s Series A extension led by SGInnovate in January. 

With the latest round, Botsync’s total funding has moved past the $20 Mn mark, it said. 

Most of the fresh capital will go towards upgrading Botsync’s MAG mobile robots and adding AI features to SyncOS, its software for coordinating robots and other factory equipment. The new features will help manufacturers increase throughput, predict maintenance needs, and analyse operational data.

How Botsync Makes Money

Founded in 2017 by Nanyang Technological University graduates Rahul Nambiar, Nikhil Venkatesh, and Prashant Trivedi, Botsync primarily serves automotive and FMCG manufacturers that regularly move goods between production lines, storage areas, and dispatch bays. Its MAG range includes lifters, conveyors, tuggers, and forklifts and can handle loads of up to 1.5 tonnes.

Botsync sells MAG robots and SyncOS together or separately. SyncOS assigns tasks and manages traffic across Botsync’s own robots and third-party equipment, and connects them with systems such as enterprise resource planning software.

Botsync’s business model combines hardware sales and software-led automation, with customers historically having the option to purchase robots through upfront capex arrangements or adopt opex-based models to spread the cost over time. The startup has also offered subscription-based software services and explored a Robotics-as-a-Service (RaaS) model in the past. 

At a global automaker’s body shop, Botsync supplied both products. SyncOS coordinated the robots delivering parts to the assembly line. Botsync said the deployment allowed the automaker to take one forklift out of service, reassign two workers, and improve productivity by 12.5%.

Where Botsync Is Expanding 

Botsync says it has completed more than 70 projects and executed over 2 Mn production tasks at 99% uptime. Its customers include Caterpillar, Ford, Nestle, Honda, Coca-Cola, and Kimberly-Clark.

To support more deployments, Botsync plans to deepen partnerships with local systems integrators and automation providers in India, where it runs a Bengaluru office and experience centre. Overseas, it plans to expand its presence in Australia and build its US business.

This comes as the broader Indian industrial control and factory automation market, which was valued at $16.7 Bn in 2025, is projected to grow at a CAGR of 11.4% and reach $23.4 Bn by 2030, according to MarketsandMarkets. 

India’s robotics and automation market includes Addverb, GreyOrange, Anscer Robotics, and Ati Motors, alongside global automation providers. 

The Inc42 Take: Can Botsync Scale Beyond Custom Deployments?

Botsync’s proposition addresses a practical manufacturing problem – automating material movement without requiring factories to overhaul their entire infrastructure. Its combination of hardware and software, enterprise customer base and reported deployments across multiple countries provide an early indication of commercial traction.

At the same time, physical AI is emerging as a promising frontier for India’s deeptech ecosystem, as advances in AI, sensors and robotics allow machines to perceive, learn and respond to real-world environments. 

However, these startups face high hardware development and manufacturing costs, while factory deployments often require customisation to fit existing infrastructure. This can make standardisation, margin expansion and faster customer acquisition difficult. Long enterprise sales cycles, maintenance requirements, and the need for specialised engineering talent add to the operational burden.

While Botsync has demonstrated deployment traction, scaling SyncOS across diverse factory environments without extensive customisation will be critical for its success.

item.title: Humyn Labs Raises $47 Mn To Collect Training Data For Robots
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: Physical AI startup Humyn Labs has raised $47 Mn (about ₹439 Cr) to expand its data collection and robot deployment…
item.content:encoded:
Physical AI startup Humyn Labs has raised $47 Mn (about ₹439 Cr) to expand its data collection and robot deployment operations. The round comprises $26 Mn in Series A equity led by Accel and $21 Mn in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital. 

Other equity investors included Prosus, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finserv Intelligence, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Jump Trading LLC, and angel investor Anita Pramoda. 

Founded earlier this year by former Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal and Ishank Gupta, Humyn Labs collects data across more than 20 countries. It works with AI research labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models, which simulate how physical environments change in response to actions. The startup claims it crossed $50 Mn in annualised revenue within six months of starting operations.

The San Francisco-based startup plans to expand its robot deployment operations to Brazil, South Korea, and India. It also plans to strengthen its data collection hardware and processing capabilities and build out its presence in San Francisco, London, and Seoul.

Humyn Labs claims to have crossed $50 Mn in annualised revenue within six months of starting operations.

The startup plans to expand its robot deployment operations to Brazil, South Korea and India. It will also strengthen its data collection hardware and processing capabilities and expand its presence across San Francisco, London and Seoul.

Physical AI refers to AI systems that interact with the real world through robots and other machines. Unlike conventional AI models that primarily process digital information, these systems need to understand how objects move, how humans perform tasks and how to respond to changing physical environments.

For instance, a warehouse robot must learn to pick up different objects, navigate obstacles and handle materials without requiring instructions for every movement.

Humyn Labs aims to address this challenge by recording how people perform tasks across factories, warehouses, farms and homes. Its proprietary devices capture human movements and interactions, which are then converted into labelled datasets to train robotics models.

The startup also works with robotics developers to test robots in real-world environments and improve their performance.

India’s Physical AI Opportunity And The Questions Around It

The opportunity extends beyond building robots. According to a July 2026 report by Counterpoint Research, India’s data collection and annotation services for physical AI could unlock a $10 Bn revenue opportunity by 2030.

The country’s large workforce, diverse working environments and relatively low data collection costs could make it an attractive destination for companies seeking real-world training data for robotics systems.

However, the business also raises questions around privacy, consent and the ownership of training data.

Physical AI datasets can involve recordings of people inside their homes, factories and workplaces. Such footage may capture personal information, household activities, workplace processes and commercially sensitive details.

This makes informed consent, data storage and restrictions on how recordings are shared particularly important. Questions also remain around how workers are compensated and whether they retain any control over footage used to train commercial AI systems.

There is a broader labour question, too. The workers whose movements are being recorded are helping train systems that could eventually automate some of their jobs. Warehousing, packaging, assembly-line operations, cleaning and inventory management are among the activities that physical AI-powered robots could increasingly take over.

This creates a potential contradiction at the heart of the emerging industry: human labour is becoming an important input in developing technologies designed to reduce dependence on human labour.

item.title: Blinkit Brings GTA 6 To 11 Cities Ahead Of Launch
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Eternal-owned quick commerce platform Blinkit has started delivering download codes for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), the latest instalment…
item.content:encoded:
Eternal-owned quick commerce platform Blinkit has started delivering download codes for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), the latest instalment in Rockstar Games’ open-world action-adventure series, in select areas across 11 Indian cities, a day ahead of the game’s global release tomorrow.

The development was announced by CEO Albinder Dhindsa today, as the Eternal-owned platform looks to tap into demand around the launch. “It took 13 years for GTA 6 to be released. In the meantime, we built Blinkit so that you can get the game delivered in minutes,” he said.

GTA 6 is currently available on Blinkit in select areas of Delhi, Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad, Noida, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Pune, Kolkata, and Ahmedabad. The company plans to expand availability to more cities between November 18 and 19, Dhindsa added.

The deliveries will see customers receive a physical box containing a digital download code for the game, rather than a traditional game disc. Buyers can redeem the code through the PlayStation Store and download the game before it unlocks in India at midnight tonight. 

Rockstar Games is releasing GTA 6 on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, while Blinkit’s listing is for PS5. The quick commerce platform is offering the PS5 Standard Edition of GTA 6 for ₹5,999. 

From Ambulances To GTA 6: Blinkit Looks Beyond Groceries  

Blinkit has increasingly used unconventional launches and quirky campaigns to stretch the idea of what a quick commerce platform can deliver.

In January 2025, the company launched a 10-minute ambulance service in parts of Gurugram, initially deploying five ambulances equipped with oxygen cylinders, defibrillators, emergency medicines and paramedics. It also ventured into document services, allowing users to order printouts and passport-size photographs through the app. 

Blinkit also launched a ‘Scream for Ice Cream’ challenge, allowing users to scream into their phones to unlock discounts on ice cream brands. The campaign turned a routine purchase into a social media-driven activity. 

These launches help Blinkit stand out in the increasingly crowded quick commerce market, where it competes with Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Flipkart Minutes, Amazon Now and BigBasket. 

India’s quick commerce market is projected to reach $40 Bn by 2030, driven by hyperlocal fulfillment (typically under 10-30 minutes) through dark stores and rapid expansion beyond groceries into higher-margin categories, as per Swiggy CEO Sriharsha Majety.

In Q2 FY27, Blinkit’s net order value rose 79.3% YoY to ₹20,940 Cr, while revenue grew 93.6% YoY to ₹19,152 Cr. The business posted an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹184 Cr against a loss of ₹156 Cr a year earlier. 

Blinkit added 308 dark stores on a net basis during the quarter, taking its network to 2,751. Eternal expects the count to cross 3,500 by March 2027 and reach about 5,000 by March 2028.

item.title: Xiaomi Faces Fresh Tax Scrutiny Over Royalty Payments
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Chinese phone manufacturer Xiaomi is reportedly facing fresh scrutiny from Indian tax authorities, with allegations of the company, as well…
item.content:encoded:
Chinese phone manufacturer Xiaomi is reportedly facing fresh scrutiny from Indian tax authorities, with allegations of the company, as well as its ex-contract manufacturer Flex, not disclosing royalty arrangements. 

In front of the Supreme Court, the Central Government said that phone maker provided relevant licensing agreements only after investigators began examining its import transactions. The authorities are seeking to recover unpaid customs duties and penalties in a dispute that could cost Xiaomi’s India business more than $150 Mn, as per a report by Reuters.

The dispute centres on whether royalty payments made by Xiaomi to technology partners should be included in the assessable value of imported smartphone components for calculating customs duties.

The company, on the other hand, has maintained that the components were imported by its contract manufacturers and that royalty payments, estimated at 2-5%, were separate transactions that should not attract customs duties.

The government has also challenged a separate plea filed by Flextronics Technologies India, the Indian arm of US-listed Flex, which has denied helping Xiaomi undervalue imports.

Flex’s challenge relates to an Indian tax tribunal’s observation that contract manufacturers had willingly participated in the layering of transactions. In September, the government had argued that Flex was liable for failing to disclose the underlying contractual arrangements to customs authorities.

Inc42 has reached out to Xiaomi for comments. The story will be updated on receiving a response.

The latest customs dispute adds to Xiaomi’s regulatory challenges in India, where the company is also facing scrutiny over its business model and compliance with foreign investment regulations.

Earlier in September, the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) reportedly recommended a detailed investigation into alleged irregularities in Xiaomi’s business operations and possible FEMA violations.

The proposed investigation is expected to examine the movement of funds between Xiaomi and related entities, its foreign investors and beneficial ownership, compliance with foreign direct investment (FDI) rules, and possible discrepancies in financial statements and auditor reports.

The SFIO proposal also reportedly called for examining Xiaomi’s relationships with sellers and ecommerce platforms, including whether preferential and exclusive product launches on select platforms violated India’s ecommerce FDI policy.

In January 2022, the government issued three show-cause notices to Xiaomi and sought ₹653 Cr in customs duties for the period between April 2017 and June 2020.

Separately, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) seized ₹5,551 Cr from Xiaomi India’s bank accounts in 2022 under FEMA provisions. The agency alleged that the company had illegally remitted funds overseas in the name of royalty payments.

The customs dispute could have implications beyond Xiaomi, as a ruling in favour of Indian authorities may invite greater scrutiny of royalty arrangements between companies and contract manufacturers across sectors such as pharmaceuticals, automobiles and electronics manufacturing.

item.title: Soket AI Raises $4 Mn From Bajaj Finserv To Expand Its AI Model Horizon
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: AI startup Soket AI has raised $4 Mn (around ₹37 Cr) from Bajaj Finserv’s applied research and innovation initiative Finserv…
item.content:encoded:
AI startup Soket AI has raised $4 Mn (around ₹37 Cr) from Bajaj Finserv’s applied research and innovation initiative Finserv Intelligence, and Pennant Technologies. The startup is working on building indigenous foundation models focused on mathematics, coding and reasoning.

Bajaj Finance invested approximately $2 Mn in the startup, while Pennant Technologies, an investee company of Bajaj Finance, invested another $2 Mn in the round.

Bajaj Finance Vice Chairman and MD Rajeev Jain said, “With Soket AI, we look forward to enabling India’s indigenous AI ecosystem, engaging with frontier research at an early stage, and bringing our scale and domain expertise to turn this research into practical solutions.”

Backed by the government’s IndiaAI Mission, Soket AI recently launched EKA-1, a 26-Bn-parameter foundation model under Project EKA, its flagship sovereign AI initiative. The funding comes as the startup looks to scale its foundation model research and develop AI systems for sectors such as financial services, cybersecurity, defence and enterprise technology.

Besides, the $4 Mn investment will support applied AI research and enterprise deployments, particularly across financial services, cybersecurity, defence and enterprise technology. 

Besides financial backing, the strategic investment is expected to open opportunities for applied AI research enterprise applications and capability building by combining Bajaj Finance’s industry expertise with Soket AI’s foundational research capabilities. 

Founded in 2019 by Abhishek Upperwal, Soket AI is building a sovereign open-source AI stack that serves a gamut of Indian languages. Speaking to Inc42 earlier this year, the founder said that the idea is to crack the AI model for India first.

Soket is among a limited set of Indian AI startups developing indigenous foundation models with support from the IndiaAI Mission. Earlier this month, ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations also launched Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B, two open-source multilingual models supporting English and 10 Indian languages.

Unlike Soket’s reasoning-focused EKA-1, ZenteiQ’s models are designed as lightweight AI assistants that can run on-premises and on edge devices, including smartphones, without requiring continuous cloud connectivity.

Meanwhile, AI unicorn Sarvam AI has also expanded its model portfolio with the launch of Prism, an open-weight decision model built on its Sarvam 105B model. The model is designed for enterprise workflows such as customer support routing, security checks and evaluating AI agent activity.

item.title: Deeptech Startup Enerzolve To Raise $20 Mn From Jungle Ventures, Others
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: Bengaluru-based deeptech startup Enerzolve Smart Technologies is in talks to raise around $16- 20 Mn (₹150-186 Cr) in a fresh…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based deeptech startup Enerzolve Smart Technologies is in talks to raise around $16- 20 Mn (₹150-186 Cr) in a fresh funding round led by existing investor Jungle Ventures, sources familiar with the development told Inc42.

The round is also expected to see participation from other existing investors, while there is a possibility of a new investor joining the startup’s cap table, the sources said. The name of the new investor is yet to be determined.

Inc42 reached out to Enerzolve and Jungle Ventures for comments on the deal. The story will be updated based on their response.

The proposed round comes less than a year after Enerzolve raised $5.1 Mn in a seed funding round co-led by Jungle Ventures and Kae Capital in January 2026. The latest fundraise, if completed, would mark a significant jump in the capital raised by the startup as it looks to scale its energy infrastructure business.

The startup had earmarked its erstwhile raised seed capital to scale manufacturing, securing certifications for its smart grid and energy storage product lines, and strengthening its engineering and product development capabilities.

It also planned to deepen its business development efforts and build relationships with utilities, EPC companies, private DISCOMs and storage developers.

Founded in 2024 by Abhay Adya and Anupam Kumar Bhatt, Enerzolve builds semiconductor-powered hardware and embedded systems for smart grids, renewable energy infrastructure and battery storage.

Its product portfolio spans three segments — instrumentation, power electronics and energy storage. These include smart meters, protection relays, grid analysers, battery management systems, power conversion systems and inverters.

The startup also offers original design manufacturing (ODM), system integration and customised engineering solutions for utilities, industrial players and infrastructure companies. The B2B firm targets clients in segments like DISCOM, EPC and battery storage developers.

It is also working on developing its core intellectual property across silicon, firmware and power electronics.

The proposed fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in India’s energy infrastructure and hardware ecosystem. The expansion of renewable energy capacity, smart meter deployments and battery energy storage projects is creating demand for indigenous power electronics and grid management solutions.

For Enerzolve, the fresh capital could help accelerate product development, manufacturing capabilities and commercial deployments as it looks to establish itself in India’s evolving energy infrastructure market.

item.title: Recove Ventures Nets ₹56 Cr To Expand Recycling Business
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Bengaluru-based Recove Ventures has raised ₹56.3 Cr (slightly over $6 Mn) in a funding round from investors like Samara Capital’s…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based Recove Ventures has raised ₹56.3 Cr (slightly over $6 Mn) in a funding round from investors like Samara Capital’s CEO Sumeet Narang, Capri Global, Amit Prakash Sharma Family Trust, 5F World’s Ganesh Natarajan and Chaitanya Kejriwal (Parkson’s Packaging).

Out of the total capital raise, ₹36.3 Cr came by way of equity allotment and the remaining is debt. 

The recycling startup plans to invest in spreading its infrastructure in Maharashtra and expand its footprint in Karnataka. 

The startup is targeting investments of over ₹2,000 Cr across Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh over the next decade. It has signed 10-year MoUs with the governments of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh, each involving proposed investments of more than ₹500 Cr. 

Founded in 2024 by Viral Chhajer, Kunal Kumar, Aayush Killa and Sharan Subaiah, Recove recycles plastic waste and sells it to companies that use such plastic to make new products. The startup claims to source its plastic waste from over 200 suppliers and sells its recycled plastic to over 40 customers. 

The startup is expanding across collection, segregation, washing and granulation. Its approach is to source and pre-process waste closer to where it is generated before moving it to larger facilities for further processing.

It currently operates a washing facility at Harohalli in Bengaluru, which procures around 600 tonnes of  plastic monthly as well as a pre-processing unit in Pune. Three more facilities are under development. 

Of this, a granulation plant at Maharashtra’s Jalgaon is expected to produce a monthly capacity of 1,100 tonnes. For context, granulation is the process of grinding plastic scrap into small, uniform pieces.

The two year old startup sees a goldmine in waste plastic, claiming that billions of dollars worth recyclable plastic go to landfills each year in India. It sees a market opportunity of over $4 Bn up for grabs, and believes its organised supply chain infra could help save up a significant chunk of the $36 Bn plastic waste between 2025-30.

However, the opportunity spans multiple waste streams, including electronic waste and metals, with businesses building solutions across collection, processing, material recovery and compliance.

For instance, waste-management platform Recykal, which raised $23 Mn, is digitising waste management. Cricketer Sachin Tendulkar also backed Recykal justed a few days ago.

Other startups are targeting different parts of the value chain. ScrapUncle raised ₹22 Cr in January 2026 to expand its waste collection and fulfilment infrastructure across Delhi-NCR. Similarly,  Karo Sambhav secured ₹56 Cr from Rainmatter in June 2026 to scale its recycling infrastructure for recovering critical and high-value materials from end-of-life products.

item.title: Egg Brand Henfruit Raises $15 Mn In First External Funding Round
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Egg brand Henfruit has raised $15 Mn (about ₹140 Cr) in a Series A round from Lok Capital, DSG Consumer…
item.content:encoded:
Egg brand Henfruit has raised $15 Mn (about ₹140 Cr) in a Series A round from Lok Capital, DSG Consumer Partners, and RPSG Capital Ventures. 

The round marks the company’s first external fundraise since Tarun Gupta founded it in 2014.

Henfruit said it will use the capital to widen its online and offline distribution across India, expand production capacity, and scale its supply chain. The company says it processes over 4 Cr eggs a month, serves customers in 15 cities, and employs more than 300 people. It expects revenue to exceed ₹350 Cr in FY27.

The brand sells through its website and platforms including Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Blinkit, and Milkbasket. Its products are also available on BigBasket, Amazon India, and Flipkart.

Henfruit uses traceability and testing to distinguish its products in India’s largely unorganised egg market. The company says it conducts daily quality tests through its own lab and independent third-party labs, and publishes the results on its website.

The fundraise comes amid growing consumer interest in branded and quality-assured food products, with food safety and transparency gaining importance in the FMCG sector. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also stepped up scrutiny of food brands over misleading advertisements, unsubstantiated product claims and labelling violations, issuing more than 150 notices to food companies in recent months.

The increased regulatory focus has put greater emphasis on quality checks, traceability and transparency across the food value chain.

Meanwhile, investor interest in India’s consumer brands has also picked up, with startups in the food and snacking segments raising capital to expand manufacturing capabilities and strengthen distribution.

Last month, healthy snacking startup Troovy raised ₹100 Cr ($10.5 Mn) in a Series B round led by Fireside Ventures to expand manufacturing capacity, invest in R&D and strengthen its quick commerce and offline distribution. 

Before that, D2C nutrition and dietary supplements startup Ace Blend raised $9.9 Mn to fund clinical trials, strengthen its supply chain, invest in R&D and develop new nutrition formats. 

Last year, Henfruit’s rival Eggoz raised $20 Mn in a Series C round led by Gaja Capital.

item.title: How Optimizely Hack Exposed 178 Websites To Crypto, Card Theft
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: In another major cybersecurity incident, malicious code injected into websites through digital experience platform (DXP) Optimizely exposed visitors to potential…
item.content:encoded:
In another major cybersecurity incident, malicious code injected into websites through digital experience platform (DXP) Optimizely exposed visitors to potential theft of cryptocurrency, payment card details and browser data.

The attack affected 178 organisations, including Zoom, BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax and Ledger, after attackers compromised customer projects on Optimizely Web and used the platform’s content delivery network (CDN) to distribute malware.

The injected JavaScript also had capabilities to deliver two iOS exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, potentially exposing visitors using vulnerable Apple devices to further attacks.

The attack was detected on November 16 by cybersecurity firm Report URI, which found 188 compromised JavaScript snippets linked to 178 organisations across 20 sectors, including banking, technology, retail, media, healthcare and telecommunications. The findings emerged from an analysis of 1,611 distinct Optimizely snippets.

The malware could replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with those controlled by attackers, capture payment card details, steal browser cookies and take screenshots of visitors’ webpages.

The attackers had received around $7,040 in cryptocurrency by November 16. Report URI revised this figure to approximately $7,151 in an update published on November 17.

In response to an Inc42 query, Optimizely said it identified the incident on November 16, 2026, after an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely Experimentation to inject malicious JavaScript into some customer projects.

The company said it had contained the incident and fully remediated the vulnerability.

As part of its response, Optimizely blocked access to the vulnerable path, deployed a fix and removed the injected code from affected projects. It also ended active sessions, revoked tokens and reset access for affected user accounts.

“We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered through Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation. We have notified and are supporting all affected customers,” the company said.

The Mechanics Of The Optimizely Attack

Optimizely Web allows businesses to experiment with different versions of their websites, personalise visitor experiences and analyse how users interact with their pages.

To use the platform, customers integrate a JavaScript snippet hosted on Optimizely’s CDN into their websites. The snippet also includes an optional field called Project JavaScript, which allows customers to add custom code that runs on their webpages.

According to Report URI, attackers exploited access to customer projects to inject malicious JavaScript into these fields.

As a result, visitors did not need to click suspicious links or visit unfamiliar websites to encounter the malware. Their browsers automatically loaded the compromised code when they accessed affected websites.

Three variations of the injected code were traced. The first loaded a malicious script directly from an external domain, while the second concealed the domain using Base64 encoding. The third contained the entire malicious payload and could execute it through a function called eval if access to the external domain was blocked.

The compromised code was also found in Zoom’s Optimizely snippet, which instructed visitors’ browsers to load another JavaScript file from the malicious domain.

However, how the attackers gained access to multiple customer projects remains unclear. Possible explanations include a compromise of Optimizely’s systems or the use of stolen credentials that allowed attackers to access customer accounts.

What Could The Malware Do?

The injected JavaScript, identified as track.js, was capable of carrying out multiple forms of malicious activity. Depending on the visitor’s device and activity on a webpage, it could target financial information, collect browsing data or attempt to exploit Apple devices.

Replacing cryptocurrency wallet addresses: One of the malware’s key capabilities was to interfere with cryptocurrency transactions.

For instance, a visitor could copy a wallet address displayed on a website, only for the malware to replace it with an address controlled by the attackers before the user pasted it into their wallet.

The script could scan webpages for cryptocurrency wallet addresses and substitute them with the attackers’ addresses. It supported several cryptocurrencies and networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Tron, Toncoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin.

Stealing payment card details: The malware could also function as a payment card skimmer, capturing information entered by visitors into website forms.

It monitored form submissions and outgoing network requests to identify payment card details, including card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs. The captured information could then be transmitted to an external server controlled by the attackers.

However, the malware had a limitation. It could not access card details entered into hosted payment iframes operated by providers such as Stripe and Adyen. Details entered directly into a website’s own payment fields were potentially exposed.

Stealing cookies and screenshots: The malware could also collect information associated with visitors’ browsing sessions.

When it detected cryptocurrency addresses alongside wallet-related or payment-related terms, it could transmit information such as the webpage URL, non-HttpOnly cookies, original wallet addresses and a screenshot of the webpage to the attackers’ server.

Delivering iOS exploit kits: The malware could also target visitors using Apple devices, particularly iPhones and iPads, by delivering two iOS exploit kits called Coruna and DarkSword.

These exploit kits are designed to exploit vulnerabilities in Apple’s operating system. The script first checked the iOS version running on a visitor’s device before attempting to load the relevant exploit chain.

The exploit kits were delivered through hidden iframes and external domains controlled by the attackers.

Devices running iOS 18.7.3 and later, as well as iOS 26.3 and later, were patched against the relevant vulnerabilities, based on comments found in the exploit kit.

Edited by Akshit Pushkarna

item.title: AI’s Social Layer & Sarvam’s Token Factory
item.dc:creator: Ankush Das
item.description: In the web era, we operated and connected through distinct platforms, each catering to a specific user need. Search engines…
item.content:encoded:
In the web era, we operated and connected through distinct platforms, each catering to a specific user need. Search engines were for information, social networks for people, marketplaces for shopping and messaging apps for conversations.

But AI assistants have begun to disrupt it all, including the web itself. Today, anyone looking for a new phone may no longer need to search Google, review websites or compare products across multiple tabs. Instead, they can turn to an AI assistant to evaluate options, compare prices and get personalised recommendations. 

The next stop for AI assistants could very well be social media platforms that have long controlled online discovery through their proprietary algorithms. 

As AI increasingly takes over product discovery, recommendations and decision-making, platforms that depend on search traffic, user attention and algorithmic distribution could find their influence under threat. But what does it really mean for startups reliant on clicks, engagement and advertising? And is AI entering a social era? Let’s answer these questions in today’s edition of The AI Shift.

The Social Feed Is Losing Its Grip

Social media giants such as Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok built their dominance around algorithm-driven feeds, determining what users discover, engage with and buy. 

Whether it is a friend’s post, a creator’s video, a trending topic or a product recommendation, these platforms have largely controlled what appears on users’ screens. AI assistants, however, are beginning to challenge this model by putting user intent ahead of algorithmic discovery. 

Instead of scrolling through multiple feeds or websites, users can simply ask an AI assistant what they want to know or buy. They can then get recommendations based on reviews, pricing, specifications and personal preferences.

Kushal Bhagia, founding partner at All In Capital, believes traditional discovery mechanisms and top-of-funnel platforms could be among the biggest casualties if AI assistants become the primary interaction layer.

His argument is that much of the social internet depends on curated feeds, algorithmic discovery and SEO-driven aggregation. If an AI assistant can retrieve, summarise and contextualise information directly, users may avoid visiting websites.

“Businesses whose primary value is helping users discover something could face pressure,” Bhagai said.

The shift is already visible in ecommerce. With the rollout of Businesses in ChatGPT, OpenAI now allows eligible businesses to claim their profiles and share product information. Eligible ecommerce and online-service businesses in the US can also create Business Agents that interact directly with customers. 

If adoption in India continues to grow beyond its current level, then OpenAI is very likely to offer this to India and other geographies. With businesses talking directly to users through these agents, the social layer may very well lose its place in today’s commerce value chain. 

AI In The Social Circle

Having said that, AI assistants may not replace social media platforms altogether, but they are fundamentally changing how people interact online. 

Social media platforms have traditionally connected users with friends, communities and content creators, and AI chatbots are increasingly becoming spaces for conversations, companionship and even emotional support.

WARC’s 2026 Consumer Trends research points to the growing use of AI chatbots for social fulfilment, including companionship and mental-health support.

This emerging trend is also backed by academic research. A study published in Nature Human Behaviour in August 2026 examined 1,131 US adults who used Character.AI, alongside thousands of chat sessions. It found that users with smaller offline social networks were more likely to report companionship as their primary reason for using AI chatbots.

Another study published in the same journal in September analysed more than 54,000 posts from Replika and ChatGPT communities. It found evidence of emotional attachment to AI systems, especially when the chatbots changed in ways they disliked.

These findings suggest that AI assistants are beginning to occupy a space that has traditionally belonged to those close to users, a job that was thus far held by social networks, messaging platforms and personal relationships.

This means that social media could increasingly serve as a destination for entertainment, content consumption and community engagement, while AI assistants become a more personalised interface for conversations, advice and decision-making.

In effect, AI assistants could evolve from tools that help users find information into platforms that people turn to for interaction, companionship and guidance.

When AI Agents Take The Wheel

The bigger shift could come when AI assistants go beyond recommendations and start taking action on behalf of users. For instance, an AI agent could book flights, compare insurance policies, negotiate purchases or analyse investment options. Instead of visiting multiple websites and apps, users could simply tell an AI agent what they want and let it handle the process.

Today, most online activities require people to search, compare, click, fill out forms and complete transactions themselves. AI agents could take over many of these tasks, changing how businesses interact with their customers.

OpenAI’s Dots offers a glimpse of this future. These always-on AI agents can connect to thousands of applications, work towards users’ goals and learn their preferences over time. One can imagine a similar future for other personal agents like Muse or Instinct. 

And for AI startups, this shift presents both challenges and opportunities.

Businesses that rely heavily on social media algorithms, advertising and user engagement to attract customers could face pressure. However, startups with loyal communities, unique content and strong customer relationships may be better placed to retain users.

Anuj Gupta, founder and CEO of KiteFishAI, an AI startup that builds compact open-weight small language models, sees opportunities emerging in areas such as agent-to-agent commerce, AI-driven communities, digital identities and systems that establish trust between autonomous AI agents.

Meanwhile, Bhagia expects businesses to start earning revenue through personalised recommendations, transaction fees and commerce conducted by AI agents. Simply put: companies may soon have to compete not just for the attention of people, but also for the attention of AI agents acting on their behalf.

The Weekly Buzz: Sarvam’s Token Factory Takes Aim At India’s AI Inference Market

Sarvam AI has launched Token Factory, an inference platform that allows developers and enterprises to access multiple AI models through a single API, without having to build and manage their own GPU infrastructure. In simple terms, Sarvam is offering the computing layer that runs AI models and generates responses, with inference taking place on GPUs operated by Sarvam in India. The platform includes Sarvam 105B alongside open models such as DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi and Gemma. 

The bigger proposition is around cost, speed and localisation. Sarvam says its serving stack uses techniques such as cache-aware routing, separate prefill and decode infrastructure and multi-tier caching to make inference faster and more efficient. It is also offering serverless and dedicated capacity, giving enterprises different ways to consume the infrastructure. For Indian businesses handling sensitive workloads, the fact that inference can happen within India could be another draw, particularly as data residency and compliance become bigger considerations.

However, Sarvam is entering a market that already has both Indian and global competition. OpenRouter, recently acquired by Stripe, has built a popular model-routing layer that gives developers access to hundreds of models through a unified API, while Indian players such as JarvisLabs and Simplismart are building their own inference offerings. JarvisLabs focuses on simplifying access to open models, whereas Simplismart has pushed further into model serving, optimisation and dedicated infrastructure. Sarvam’s differentiation therefore rests partly on combining its own models, India-based infrastructure and an inference stack optimised for its workloads.

The bigger challenge will be proving that this advantage translates into better economics and reliability at production scale. Model access itself is becoming increasingly commoditised, and developers can switch between providers relatively easily. Sarvam will need to show that its infrastructure can consistently deliver competitive latency, token costs and model availability while handling large enterprise workloads. If it can, Token Factory could become more than another model API and potentially form part of the infrastructure layer powering India’s emerging AI application and agent ecosystem.

Top Stories From India & Around The World

  • OpenAI Brings Inference To India: The program will allow businesses to process supported GPT-6 Luna workloads within the country. The move addresses data localisation requirements that have been a barrier to AI adoption among regulated businesses and increases competition for Indian AI companies offering locally hosted models.
  • Bharat Semi Raises $24 Mn: The Bengaluru-based semiconductor startup’s seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons and Indus Bridge Ventures. It will use the capital to develop low-power, low-latency sensors for physical AI applications and expand its engineering teams.
  • MeitY Reviews Physical AI Data Collection: The ministry has sought details from Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company over their collection and use of gig workers’ video and sensor data for training physical AI models, highlighting concerns around worker consent, consumer privacy and the transfer of Indian training data overseas.
  • AI Giants Face Lawsuit: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX’s AI division are facing a lawsuit from nonprofit groups seeking to halt the development of increasingly advanced AI systems, arguing that the companies have failed to demonstrate adequate control over frontier models.
  • How Deep Is Nvidia’s AI Ecosystem In India? Nvidia’s AI ecosystem in India is expanding beyond GPU sales, with the chipmaker increasingly embedded across the country’s AI infrastructure, cloud, data centre and startup landscape. 

Startup In The Spotlight: ByteAsk

Founded in 2026 by IIT Delhi alumni Anirudha Kulkarni and Pratyush Saini,, ByteAsk is building an AI coding agent focused on C and C++, two programming languages widely used in mission-critical systems across defence, automobiles, aerospace, medical technology and financial services sectors.

While AI coding tools have largely focused on mainstream software development, organisations working with C and C++ often face additional challenges around performance, reliability, security and legacy code. ByteAsk is designed to help developers in these environments use AI for software development without compromising control over sensitive code and intellectual property.

The platform supports both open- and closed-source AI models and can be deployed entirely on-premise, allowing enterprises to keep their code and data within their own infrastructure. The startup is developing two offerings, ByteAsk Harness and a B2B enterprise product, with a focus on making AI-assisted C/C++ development more reliable rather than simply generating code.

ByteAsk has raised $1 Mn from Y Combinator and follows a subscription-led business model complemented by enterprise services. The startup is targeting the growing AI coding market, estimated at ~11 Bn in annualised value as of April 2026, while carving out a niche around C/C++ and the performance-critical systems where these languages remain central.

Prompt Of The Week

What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work? 

Here’s Mashhood Raza Azka, CEO of VoxForce.ai, with a prompt he uses to work out where AI-powered Human Agents can improve customer engagement across digital channels.

“You are an expert in AI-powered Human Agents, customer experience strategy and business process transformation.

Here is our situation: We are a business looking to improve customer engagement across our digital channels. Our customers interact with us for product discovery, sales enquiries, support, appointments and service requests. We want to understand how AI-powered Human Agents can handle these interactions through natural voice and video conversations.

I need you to:

  • Identify customer-facing processes where AI-powered Human Agents can deliver the greatest business value.
  • Recommend suitable AI Agent personas for sales, customer support, reception, product advisory and lead qualification.
  • Map how these agents should understand customer intent, respond to queries and guide conversations towards meaningful outcomes.
  • Identify opportunities to integrate lead capture, appointment scheduling, product recommendations and payment workflows into conversations.
  • Define when an AI Agent should resolve an interaction independently and when it should hand over to a human.
  • Highlight the knowledge, integrations and safeguards required for reliable AI Agent performance.
  • Recommend measurable KPIs to assess engagement, customer satisfaction, lead conversion and operational efficiency.

Prioritise recommendations based on business impact, implementation feasibility and customer experience. Keep the output specific, practical and execution-oriented.”
